$comment: State names, two-letter abbreviations, and multi-state regions, lifted verbatim from
signals.py. Values are the canonical Title-cased display labels.
ABBREVIATIONS ARE MATCHED CASE-SENSITIVELY and that is load-bearing: a case-insensitive
'up'/'mp' collides with shop-floor phrasing like 'set up' / 'setup' and would corrupt the
profile. 'UP' written in caps is a state. This is why `abbreviations` carries flags ""
while `names` carries "i".
Regions are WHOLE PHRASES only — 'south' and 'india' on their own say nothing
('south side me rehta hu', 'made in India'), so neither is a cue.
`administrative` IS A PICKER LIST, NOT A DETECTOR (#1429), and the split is deliberate.
`names`, `abbreviations` and `regions` are DETECTION data: signals.py compiles them into
regexes that run over free worker speech, so every entry added there changes what is read
out of a sentence and can change the cross-language utterances corpus. `administrative` is
read by nothing in either detector — it exists so a UI can offer a closed, complete list of
the 28 states and 8 union territories to pick from.
THEY DIFFER, AND THE DIFFERENCE IS THE POINT. `names` holds 22 entries and no union
territory, because it only ever needed the states a worker says out loud. A picker cannot
have that gap: Delhi and Chandigarh are canonical manufacturing-hub cities in cities.json
with nowhere to sit. Adding them to `names` instead would make 'Delhi' resolve as a STATE in
free text, where it is far more often the city — a detection change smuggled in behind a UI
feature. Hence a separate key.
administrative: Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu
